questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a formal analysis describes
questions.learningObjective: describe what a formal analysis sets out to establish
questions.stem: A clinician's note records the arrangement of colour, shape, line and value in a canvas, without naming the scene it shows.

options.text: It is a formal analysis, which describes the visible elements in their arrangement
It is an iconographic reading, which identifies the objects that carry the meaning
options.misconception: mistakes a description of form for an identification of symbols

options.text: It is a contextual reading, which dates the canvas from the events around it
options.misconception: mistakes a description of form for a historical setting

options.text: It is a psychological reading, which infers the artist's state of mind
options.misconception: mistakes a description of form for an inference about the painter

questions.explanation: A formal analysis sets out the elements of the work and how they are arranged, without naming what is depicted. That is the difference between describing the picture and interpreting what it means.
questions.hint: Ask whether the note names what is depicted.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a formal analysis cannot settle
questions.learningObjective: identify what a formal analysis is able and unable to settle
questions.stem: A note records that the canvas shows a line of five figures and a diagonal of light, but says nothing about who they are or what they do.

options.text: The note is iconographic, so it settles the identities of the five figures
options.misconception: claims a formal note identifies the figures

options.text: The note is formal, so it settles how the picture looks but not what it means
The note is contextual, so it settles the date of the commission
options.misconception: claims a formal note dates the work

options.text: The note is complete, so nothing further can usefully be asked of the picture
options.misconception: confuses one kind of analysis with the whole task

questions.explanation: Describing line, light and the arrangement of figures is formal analysis, and it leaves the question of identity and meaning open. Formal analysis is one reading among several, not the end of the enquiry.
questions.hint: Ask what the note still leaves unanswered.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an iconographic reading identifies
questions.learningObjective: explain what an iconographic reading actually establishes
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of what an iconographic reading of a painting actually establishes.

answer.exemplar: An iconographic reading identifies the conventional signs by which a subject is recognised: the attributes, emblems and events that in a given tradition stand for a particular figure or story. It then names the subject those signs point to, and it can check its own conclusions by asking whether every attribute fits. What it establishes is the subject of the work, not the artist's intention, the patron's wishes or the circumstances of the commission, all of which remain separate lines of evidence.

questions.explanation: Iconographic reading identifies the conventional signs and names the subject they point to, checking that the attributes fit. It settles the subject, not intention, patronage or circumstance.
questions.hint: Ask what the signs point to, not what the painter meant.

questions.topic: Attributes used to settle a subject
questions.learningObjective: calculate the proportion of figures standing in the foreground
questions.stem: A note records that a panel contains seven figures, of whom four stand in the foreground and three in the middle ground.
questions.explanation: Four of the seven figures are in the foreground, so the ratio is 4 divided by 7, which is 0.571 to three places. Such counts describe arrangement, which is the ground formal analysis works on.
questions.hint: Divide the foreground figures by the total number.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a contextual reading brings
questions.learningObjective: identify the kind of reading that draws on circumstances around a work

stimulus.body: The clinic's note on a painting records that the canvas was hung in a room built two years after the events it appears to show, that the building belonged to a family with a documented interest in the dispute depicted, and that the same room appears in the artist's own later works.

questions.stem: From the clinic's note above, which kind of reading does this evidence amount to?

options.text: It is a formal analysis, since it counts the objects shown in the canvas
options.misconception: confuses the setting with a description of form

options.text: It is an iconographic reading, since it identifies the figures in the scene
options.misconception: confuses the setting with the identification of symbols

options.text: It is a contextual reading, since it draws on the events, ownership and setting around the work
It is a biographical reading, since it describes the life of the family that owned it
options.misconception: reduces the evidence to a story about the owners

questions.explanation: Setting, ownership and the circumstances of display are the material of contextual reading. Identification of figures would be iconographic, and counting objects formal, so the note belongs with context.
questions.hint: Ask whether the evidence concerns events or the picture's own form.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission record as evidence
questions.learningObjective: assess what a commission record contributes that the work cannot show
questions.stem: A clinician's note asks what a commission record contributes that the picture itself cannot show.

options.text: It settles the subject, because the client always wrote down the iconography
options.misconception: believes the client's record overrides the picture's signs

options.text: It records the colour scheme, so the picture's palette can be reconstructed exactly
options.misconception: claims the record contains the painting's own visual data

options.text: It proves the artist worked alone, because a named assistant never appears in it
options.misconception: reads silence in the record as proof of working alone

options.text: It records what was asked for, what was paid for and what was agreed, as external evidence

questions.explanation: A commission record is external evidence of the terms of the work, which the picture cannot testify to on its own. It can confirm what was asked for and paid, but it neither replaces the picture nor settles its iconography.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of evidence the record is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The risk in a biographical reading
questions.learningObjective: identify the chief danger of explaining a work through an artist's life
questions.stem: A clinic note asks what the chief danger is when a reader explains a picture through the artist's biography.

options.text: That a biography is always shorter than the account the picture deserves
options.misconception: measures the problem in length rather than in method

options.text: That the life story is used to fill gaps the picture cannot fill, and does the explaining
That a biography will in time be corrected by better archives
options.misconception: treats the risk as a temporary one about records

options.text: That a reader who knows the life will always overvalue the picture
options.misconception: makes the risk a matter of taste rather than of reasoning

questions.explanation: Biographical reading is at its weakest when the life story is used to stand in for what the picture cannot yet explain, so the context closes the enquiry down. The risk is that a tidy narrative substitutes for evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the biography is doing the work the picture should do.

questions.topic: The assumption inside a psychological reading
questions.learningObjective: weigh dated evidence used to support a reading of a sitter's state of mind
questions.stem: A note cites three documented episodes in a sitter's life and treats the dates of two of them as evidence of the state of mind shown in the portrait.

options.text: The dates prove nothing at all, since a portrait never records a life
options.misconception: dismisses all context as irrelevant to a picture

options.text: The dates prove the reading, because they come from the archival record
options.misconception: treats documentary fact as proof of an interpretation

options.text: The dates may support a reading, but the link between a date and a feeling is an assumption
The dates identify the sitter's occupation, which is what the portrait shows
options.misconception: confuses dating evidence with identification of subject

questions.explanation: Dated episodes are solid facts, but the step from a date to a state of mind is interpretive and needs stating as such. A reader should be told which link in the argument is fact and which is inference.
questions.hint: Ask which step in the argument is inference.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a formal analysis describes
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a descriptive note from an interpretive one
questions.stem: A clinician weighs two notes on one canvas: one records only line, colour and arrangement, the other names the figures and reads a mood.

options.text: The second note is complete, so the first has nothing to add to it
options.misconception: treats one reading as exhausting the picture

options.text: Both notes are formal, since neither of them offers an account of the artist's life
options.misconception: counts the second note as formal though it interprets

options.text: Both notes are iconographic, since both treat the objects in the picture as signs
options.misconception: misclassifies a description of form as a reading of signs

options.text: The first is formal and stops at description, while the second adds interpretation on top of it

questions.explanation: The first note describes the work's elements and arrangement, which is the work of formal analysis. The second adds naming and interpretation, which rests on conventions and assumptions the note should state.
questions.hint: Ask which note goes beyond describing what is there.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a formal analysis cannot settle
questions.learningObjective: explain in writing what a formal analysis cannot establish
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of what a formal analysis cannot establish, however carefully it is carried out.

answer.exemplar: A formal analysis establishes the elements of a work and the way they are arranged: line, colour, shape, value, the balance of the composition and the direction of the light. It cannot establish who the figures are, because that depends on recognised signs and shared convention rather than on anything visible in the arrangement. Nor can it establish what the work was for, what the artist intended, or how the subject was understood by those who first saw it. All of those need evidence of a different kind.

questions.explanation: Formal analysis establishes elements and arrangement but not identity, purpose or intention, since those depend on convention, documents and context. Its limits are the point at which other kinds of reading begin.
questions.hint: Ask which questions need evidence of a different kind.

questions.topic: What an iconographic reading identifies
questions.learningObjective: calculate the proportion of objects that are conventional attributes
questions.stem: A clinic note records that a painting shows nine identifiable objects, of which four are conventional attributes of the saint depicted.
questions.explanation: Four of the nine identified objects are conventional attributes, which is 4 over 9, or 44.44 per cent to two places. A high proportion of conventional signs is what allows a subject to be named.
questions.hint: Take the fraction of nine and convert it to a percentage.

questions.topic: Attributes used to settle a subject
questions.learningObjective: identify which attributes are fit for settling a subject
questions.stem: A question asks which group of attributes is most reliable for settling the subject of a panel showing a figure with a wheel, a key and a sword.

options.text: The attributes that the artist painted most often in other surviving works
options.misconception: judges attributes by the artist's habit rather than by convention

options.text: The attributes that are conventional and specific to one recognised figure in the tradition
The attributes that the sitter in the portrait appears to be holding himself
options.misconception: confuses a formal description with a conventional attribute

options.text: The attributes that the panel's first owner wrote down in a later inventory
options.misconception: treats a later inventory as proof of conventional attributes

questions.explanation: An attribute settles a subject because it is conventional, that is because that object has an agreed association with that figure. The other three grounds are about habits, description or records, not about convention.
questions.hint: Ask what makes an attribute meaningful to others besides the painter.

questions.topic: What a contextual reading brings
questions.learningObjective: identify what a contextual reading adds to a reading of a work
questions.stem: A question asks what a contextual reading adds that the other three kinds of reading leave out.

options.text: The signs by which the subject of the work may be recognised
options.misconception: describes iconographic analysis as the contribution of context

options.text: The elements of the work and the arrangement in which they appear
options.misconception: describes formal analysis as the contribution of context

options.text: The events, circumstances and setting in which the work was made and used
The inner states the figures in the work are taken to represent
options.misconception: describes psychological analysis as the contribution of context

questions.explanation: Context brings the circumstances of the work's making and use: events, ownership, setting and later history. Form, iconography and inner states each belong to a different kind of reading.
questions.hint: Ask what the other three readings leave out.

questions.topic: A commission record as evidence
questions.learningObjective: weigh two documents that agree with each other
questions.stem: A clinic note records that a painter's diary mentions a payment on a date that the commission record for the same picture also gives.

options.text: Two documents that agree remove any need to look at the picture itself
options.misconception: believes documents make the picture unnecessary

options.text: Two documents that agree prove the subject the picture shows
options.misconception: treats agreement in dates as proof of a subject

options.text: Two documents that agree show that the diary was copied from the record
options.misconception: assumes copying as the only explanation for agreement

options.text: Two independent documents that agree strengthen the dating, and neither settles the subject

questions.explanation: Independent documents that agree give the date good support, which is what cross-checking is for. Neither agreement nor dating settles the subject, and the picture still has to be read on its own terms.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The risk in a biographical reading
questions.learningObjective: identify the unsupported step in a biographical explanation of a palette

stimulus.body: The clinic's file records that a painter's letters describe years of poverty and grief, that a panel of that period is darker than his others, and that the panel was painted in the year the letters were written.

questions.stem: From the clinic's file above, what is wrong with the link the file draws between the letters and the palette?

options.text: The link is proved, because the letters and the panel date to the same year
options.misconception: treats a shared date as proof of a connection

options.text: The link between the hardship and the palette is an assumption the note has not established
The panel proves the hardship, since the palette records what the painter felt
options.misconception: reverses the argument into a proof of the biography

options.text: The note is formal, because it describes the palette of the panel in detail
options.misconception: misclassifies a biographical claim as a formal description

questions.explanation: A shared date is a fact, but the step from documented hardship to a dark palette is an inference that the record does not make. The note should state the link as an assumption rather than present it as an explanation.
questions.hint: Ask where the link between life and paint was documented.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The assumption inside a psychological reading
questions.learningObjective: explain the assumption usually made inside a psychological reading
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of the assumption that usually sits underneath a psychological reading.

answer.exemplar: A psychological reading takes a mark on the surface and treats it as the visible sign of a state of mind: a lowered head becomes dejection, a hard stare becomes aggression, a faint colour becomes anxiety. The assumption is that an artist records inner states through visible means and that those states can be read back with any confidence. It is a strong claim, because expression is conventional and trained, so the same gesture carries very different meanings in different hands and periods.

questions.explanation: The reading assumes that visible expression reliably shows an inner state and can be read back. Expression is conventional and learned, so the same gesture can carry different meanings in different hands.
questions.hint: Ask what the reading takes the visible sign to reveal.

questions.hint: Add the three sets of attributes together.

questions.learningObjective: identify what a formal analysis is unable to establish
questions.stem: A question asks what a formal analysis of a panel cannot establish, however carefully it is done.

options.misconception: treats formal analysis as incapable of describing arrangement

options.text: The number of distinct colours used, because the eye cannot count reliably
options.misconception: claims colour counting falls outside formal analysis

options.text: The subject the picture represents, because that depends on recognised signs
The relative sizes of the shapes, because measurements are not part of form

questions.stem: A clinic note asks what an iconographic reading is designed to identify in a work.

options.text: The social class of the sitters, read from their clothes and their setting
options.misconception: confuses iconography with social interpretation

options.text: The period when the work was made, read from its style and its materials
options.misconception: confuses identification of subject with dating

options.text: The state of mind of the artist, read from the handling of the paint
options.misconception: confuses iconography with psychological reading

options.text: The subject the work represents, read through its conventional signs and attributes

questions.explanation: Iconographic reading is the business of naming a subject from its recognised signs. Dating, the artist's mind and the sitters' class are other readings, each with its own evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the signs are meant to name.

questions.learningObjective: calculate how many attributes match the best candidate subject

options.text: Three quarters of the attributes fit the best candidate, so the subject is settled
options.misconception: counts the shared attribute for only one candidate

options.text: Half of the attributes fit the best candidate, so the subject is not settled by attributes alone
All four attributes fit the best candidate, so the subject can be stated with confidence
options.misconception: counts the disputed attribute as agreeing

options.text: Only one attribute fits any candidate, so no subject can be proposed at all
options.misconception: ignores the candidate that matches two attributes

questions.explanation: Two of the four attributes match the leading candidate, which is half of them. One is disputed and one favours another figure, so the attributes do not settle the subject and further evidence is needed.
questions.hint: Compare the matching attributes with the total recorded.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a contextual reading brings
questions.learningObjective: explain how context can explain a visible choice
questions.stem: A question asks how a contextual reading can explain a choice that a formal analysis would leave as a curiosity.

options.text: By showing that the chosen arrangement is more balanced than the alternatives
options.misconception: explains a choice by formal judgement rather than by context

options.text: By showing that the painter used the same arrangement in several other works
options.misconception: explains a choice by the painter's habit rather than by circumstance

options.text: By showing that the circumstances of commission or display made the choice necessary
By showing that the sitter asked for the particular elements in the picture
options.misconception: reduces context to a single client's request

questions.explanation: A contextual reading can show that a subject, scale or setting was demanded by the commission or by the room the work was made for. It explains a visible choice by the circumstances behind it, which description alone cannot do.
questions.hint: Ask what circumstances could make a choice necessary.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The risk in a biographical reading
questions.learningObjective: explain in writing why a biographical reading is treated as risky
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of why a biographical reading is treated as a risky kind of interpretation.

answer.exemplar: A biographical reading begins with documented facts about a life and asks what they explain in a work, and the danger is that a tidy narrative will take the place of evidence. Once the painter's hardship is known, every dark passage can be read as its expression, and the work stops being examined on its own terms. The reading is sound only when a particular documented fact is tied to a particular visible feature and the connection is offered as an argument to be checked. Biography is strongest as one line of evidence among several.

questions.explanation: The risk is that a tidy life story substitutes for examining the work, so every feature gets explained by it. A biographical reading is sound only when a specific documented fact is tied to a specific visible feature.
questions.hint: Ask what a biographical reading risks replacing.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate two notes on the same portrait for their evidential standing

options.misconception: lets a record overrule the reading of the surface

options.misconception: rates internal observation above external evidence without reason

questions.explanation: Reading dejection from a lowered head assumes that expression shows an inner state directly. Documented circumstances are firmer facts but do not by themselves explain the pose, so the two notes answer different questions.
questions.hint: Ask what each note assumes and what it establishes.

options.misconception: claims the note supplies historical context

options.misconception: dismisses conventional signs as mere decoration

questions.explanation: Objects that appear together in a workshop pattern are conventional attributes, and sets of attributes are how a subject is recognised. A private code would leave the subject undecidable for anyone else.

questions.explanation: A record tells us what was asked for and agreed, which is genuine evidence, but the picture may depart from it, as pictures do. The record has to be weighed against the work rather than accepted as decisive.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The risk in a biographical reading
questions.learningObjective: explain in writing how a biographical reading can be used responsibly
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of how a biographical reading can be used responsibly.

answer.exemplar: A biographical reading is responsible when it stays with a claim that can be tested. The reader names a documented fact, points to a specific visible feature, and states the proposed link between them, so that another reader can weigh the evidence and disagree. What must be avoided is the general appeal to the artist's life as an atmosphere that explains everything, because that makes the work unfalsifiable. Used this way, the biography adds one line of evidence to the account instead of replacing it.

questions.explanation: A responsible biographical reading names a documented fact, points to a visible feature and states the link, so it can be checked and disputed. It adds evidence rather than replacing the examination of the work.
questions.hint: Ask what would let another reader dispute the reading.

questions.explanation: Reading a face involves interpreting expression, and each reader carries assumptions about what gestures mean. Two careful observers can therefore differ, and each should be asked to state the assumptions behind the reading.

questions.topic: What a contextual reading brings
questions.learningObjective: explain in writing what a contextual reading contributes
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of what a contextual reading contributes that a formal reading cannot.

answer.exemplar: A contextual reading sets the work inside the world that surrounded it: the events of the period, the circumstances of the commission, the building it hung in, the people who owned it and what happened to it afterwards. This kind of evidence can explain choices that are visible but unexplained, such as a subject that flatters a particular family or a scale that matches a specific square. The risk is that a lively context can swallow the work itself, so the reading has to keep asking what the evidence is doing to the picture rather than only to the story.

questions.explanation: Context brings the events, ownership and setting that can explain visible choices the picture alone leaves unexplained. Its risk is that the story displaces the work, so the evidence must be tied to the picture.
questions.hint: Ask what the context explains in the picture itself.

questions.hint: Ask what kind of evidence a recorded setting is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commission record as evidence
questions.learningObjective: explain in writing how a commission record can help or mislead
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of how a commission record can help or mislead a reader.

answer.exemplar: A commission record helps when it names what was ordered, by whom and for what sum, because it sets the work against expectations that were stated in advance. It can mislead when it records the first version of the terms rather than the final one, or when the client's wishes were never what the picture actually shows. A payment for a subject does not prove the subject was painted as agreed, so the record has to be read as one document among several, and compared with the picture and with other records.

questions.explanation: The record sets the work against stated expectations, which is its value. It misleads when it records earlier terms or what the client wanted rather than what was painted, so it must be read alongside the picture.
questions.hint: Ask what a payment for a subject proves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an iconographic reading identifies
questions.learningObjective: explain in writing how an iconographic reading is checked
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of how an iconographic reading is checked once a subject has been proposed.

answer.exemplar: A proposed subject is checked by asking whether the attributes present in the work are the ones conventionally associated with that figure or story, and whether the subject explains all of them rather than only the most conspicuous. A second check looks for contradictions: an attribute that belongs to a different figure, an incident that cannot belong to the subject, or a setting inconsistent with it. Where the attributes agree, the subject can be stated with some confidence; where they conflict, the reading should be recorded as open rather than tidied away.

questions.explanation: A proposed subject is checked by asking whether the attributes fit it and whether it explains them all, then by looking for contradictions. Agreement supports the subject; conflict should be recorded rather than tidied away.
questions.hint: Ask whether every attribute fits and no other one contradicts.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a formal analysis cannot settle
questions.learningObjective: explain in writing why a formal analysis is a necessary first step
questions.stem: A clinician asks for a written account of why a formal analysis is a necessary first step even though it cannot settle a subject.

answer.exemplar: A formal analysis settles the things that every later reading depends on. It establishes which colours, shapes, lines and tones are present, how they are placed, and where the weight of the composition falls, so that an iconographic argument can point to a specific device rather than to a vague impression. It also fixes the picture for comparison, since a reader who disagrees about the subject can at least agree about the arrangement. Its limits are real, but they are the limits of a first step rather than a substitute for one.

questions.explanation: Formal analysis fixes the elements and their arrangement, which later readings depend on and use to argue. It cannot settle a subject, but it is the first step rather than a substitute for one.
questions.hint: Ask what the later readings need the first reading to fix.

questions.explanation: Four of the six identified attributes are recorded in the published pattern, which is 4 over 6, or 0.667 to three places. The two unmatched attributes still need an account before the subject can be stated confidently.
questions.hint: Divide the matching attributes by the total identified.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Attributes used to settle a subject
questions.learningObjective: explain why one attribute cannot name a subject on its own
questions.stem: A question asks why an attribute that belongs to one figure is not enough to name a subject on its own.

options.text: Because attributes are only meaningful in paintings of the last hundred years
options.misconception: dates the meaning of attributes to a recent period

options.text: Because a single attribute may be shared, borrowed or added, so a set must agree
Because the subject must always be named by the artist in the picture's title
options.misconception: believes only a title can name a subject

options.text: Because attributes change meaning between centuries and so can never be used
options.misconception: concludes attributes are useless from their shifting meaning

questions.explanation: An attribute is meaningful because it is conventional, but a single one can be shared or borrowed, so a subject should be settled by a set that agrees. Their meaning shifts over time, which is a reason to check them, not to abandon them.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the attributes disagree.
